name: dcmtk
why: The DICOM toolkit opens a door into medical imaging formats and network protocols that few developers have ever touched.

brief.what_it_is: DCMTK is the OFFIS DICOM toolkit, a package of source code, documentation and build instructions for a set of software libraries and applications that implement part of the DICOM/MEDICOM medical imaging standard. The README describes it as sub-packages covering data encoding and decoding (dcmdata), image processing (dcmimgle), networking (dcmnet), JPEG and JPEG-LS compression, presentation states, structured reporting, radiology objects, a database server (dcmqrdb), and a modality worklist server (dcmwlm). The executables listed in the package metadata (for example dcmdump, dcm2img, storescu, storescp, findscu, movescu, echoscu, img2dcm, xml2dcm, dsr2html) are the command-line tools built from these libraries. The README does not describe what each tool takes in or emits, so that detail is inferred from the tool names and is unverified.
brief.why_it_exists: The README does not state a motivation. It describes the package as an implementation of part of the DICOM/MEDICOM standard, with bug reports and questions routed to the project's mailing address and forum.
brief.how_it_works: The README describes a layered set of libraries (config, oficonv, oflog, ofstd at the base, then dcmdata, dcmimgle, dcmnet and others above them) with command-line applications in each sub-directory's apps folder. The applications are thin tools over those libraries. The README does not explain the mechanism in more detail.
brief.install_notes: The README says to build and install from the INSTALL file in the repository, which I did not fetch, so build requirements are unknown. It also links a COPYRIGHT file and a HISTORY file. The README's CI badges show builds for Windows (CMake), macOS (CMake) and Linux (CMake), which suggests all three are supported. The package metadata shows the Homebrew formula installs the full set of about 80 executables. No accounts, hardware or runtime configuration are mentioned in the README.
brief.standout: It is one of the few open implementations of the DICOM networking and file standard, and it ships a very wide set of tools (from dump and convert utilities to C-STORE, C-FIND and C-MOVE clients and servers, plus a worklist server) under one package. The repository README is short and points outward to the wiki, API docs and forum rather than carrying usage examples.
brief.status: Appears maintained. The GitHub README shows Windows, macOS and Linux CI badges on the master branch, which indicates ongoing automated builds. I did not see a release date or last-commit date, so I cannot confirm the recency of releases. The homepage could not be read, so I have no further evidence.
brief.caveats: The official homepage (dcmtk.org) is behind a JavaScript bot-detection challenge and returned no content, so the brief relies on the GitHub README. The README contains no usage examples or command lines. Build and install details live in the INSTALL file, which I did not read. The README does not say which tool does what, so the writer should verify any per-tool claims against the docs before publishing. The README does not state a license in the portion I saw; it refers to a COPYRIGHT file, which I did not read, so licensing is unverified.

judge.reason: DCMTK makes the unfamiliar DICOM medical-imaging format and its network services tangible through tools for inspecting, converting, and exchanging imaging objects.

entry.title: DCMTK
entry.tldr: About 80 command-line tools for reading, converting and sending DICOM, the file and network format behind medical imaging, from one long-running open toolkit.
entry.deeper_look:
DCMTK is the OFFIS DICOM toolkit. The project's own words: "source code, documentation and installation instructions for a set of software libraries and applications implementing part of the DICOM/MEDICOM Standard." The Homebrew formula installs the command-line tools built on those libraries, roughly 80 of them.

The tool names suggest the range. There are dump and convert utilities (`dcmdump`, `dcm2img`, `dcm2json`, `dcm2xml`, `img2dcm`, `xml2dcm`), structured report converters (`dsr2html`, `dsr2xml`), and networking tools named after DICOM operations (`echoscu`, `storescu`, `storescp`, `findscu`, `movescu`). There is also a modality worklist server (`wlmscpfs`). What each one takes in and emits is inferred from the names here, so check the docs before relying on it.

The idea underneath is that medical imaging has its own world: a binary file format and a network protocol, both defined by one large standard, that most developers never touch. The README describes layered libraries, with a base of config and utility code, then `dcmdata` for encoding and decoding, `dcmimgle` for images, and `dcmnet` for networking. The command-line tools are thin programs over those layers. Reading the tools is a way into the standard.

The README gives no motivation and no usage examples. It points to a wiki, API docs and a forum for the rest.

try_this.what_happens: Prints the options for the DICOM file dumper, a first look at how the toolkit describes its own file format.
Shows the options for the DICOM network ping client, the simplest way into the protocol side.
Lists how an ordinary image can be wrapped into a DICOM file.

entry.whats_unique: It is one of the few open implementations of both the DICOM file standard and its networking, with clients, servers and converters in one package.
entry.caveats: The README has no usage examples and the homepage could not be read when this entry was researched, so expect to learn from the wiki and API docs.
